summary: The largest living land animal, a bull can stand nearly 4 m at the shoulder and weigh over 6 tonnes. Herds are led by old matriarchs whose memory of distant water and danger can decide whether a family survives a drought.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from the Sahel to South Africa, in fragmented populations
abilities: Communicates with infrasonic rumbles below human hearing that can travel several kilometres
Senses ground-borne vibrations through sensitive feet and trunk tip
Uses a boneless, muscular trunk to pluck single leaves, lift heavy logs, suck up water and snorkel
Digs wells in dry riverbeds that other animals later drink from
Clears woodland and opens grassland, shaping whole savanna landscapes

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit; may eat 150 kg or more per day
animal.habitat: Savanna, woodland, semi-desert and river valleys
animal.size: Bulls up to ~4 m at shoulder and 6–7 t; cows ~2.5–3 m and 2.5–3.5 t
animal.behaviour: Families gather around the bones of dead elephants, touching and turning them with their trunks. Matriarchs lead herds along routes remembered over decades.
fieldMarks: Largest land animal, grey and wrinkled
Very large ears shaped roughly like the map of Africa
Back dips in the middle; two finger-like tips on the trunk
Tusks curve outward and forward in both sexes
animal.voice: Trumpeting blasts, and deep rumbles, much of it too low for people to hear, that carry several kilometres
animal.lookalikes: African forest elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) is smaller with rounder ears and straighter, downward-pointing tusks. Asian elephant has small ears and a domed head. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Amboseli (Kenya), Chobe (Botswana), Kruger (South Africa) and Addo Elephant National Park
animal.season: Resident; dry-season gatherings at rivers and waterholes

lore: Pliny the Elder's Natural History (Book 8) called the elephant the animal nearest to humans in understanding. Ptolemaic Egypt captured African elephants for war, fielding them at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE.
funFact: Elephant pregnancy lasts about 22 months, the longest of any living land mammal.

summary: The largest wild cat, a solitary ambush hunter whose stripes break up its outline in tall grass and forest shade. Fewer than 6,000 remain in the wild, scattered from the Russian Far East to Sumatra.
nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Southeast Asia, Sumatra, Russian Far East and NE China
abilities: Kills prey several times its own weight, such as gaur and sambar, with a throat or nape bite
Swims strongly and readily hunts in water, as in the Sundarbans mangroves
Roars that can carry about 3 km through forest
Marks territories with scent sprays and scrapes that tell rivals its sex and status

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, wild pigs, gaur, buffalo; occasionally fish and smaller prey
animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and grasslands with dense cover and water
animal.lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild; to ~20 in captivity
animal.size: Males 180–300 kg and up to ~3 m including tail; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Hunts alone by stalking to within a few metres before a short explosive rush. Each tiger's stripe pattern is unique.
fieldMarks: Largest cat, orange with black vertical stripes
White underparts and white spots on the backs of the ears
Stripe pattern unique to each animal
animal.voice: A deep roar; a soft, snorting 'chuff' (prusten) as a friendly greeting
animal.lookalikes: Leopards have rosettes, not stripes. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Ranthambore, Bandhavgarh, Kanha and Tadoba (India); Chitwan (Nepal) — all by guided safari vehicle
animal.season: Resident; Indian parks are usually open about Oct–Jun, with sightings easiest in the hot months Apr–Jun at waterholes

lore: The Hindu goddess Durga rides a tiger into battle against the demon Mahishasura. In Chinese cosmology the White Tiger (Bai Hu) guards the West, and the tiger is the third animal of the zodiac.
funFact: The stripes are in the skin as well as the fur: a shaved tiger is still striped.

summary: A smoky-grey cat of the high mountains of Central and South Asia, so rarely seen that it is called the 'ghost of the mountains'. Its long, thick tail works as a balance pole on cliffs and a scarf when it sleeps.
nativeRange: Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, Pamir, Tian Shan, Altai and Tibetan Plateau
abilities: Lives and hunts at 3,000–5,500 m, where the air holds about half the oxygen of sea level
Leaps across ravines and down cliffs several times its own body length
Large, fur-soled paws act as snowshoes
Takes down blue sheep and ibex up to three times its own weight on steep slopes

animal.diet: Carnivore: blue sheep (bharal), Siberian ibex, argali, marmots, pikas; sometimes livestock
animal.habitat: Steep, broken alpine terrain and cliffs above the treeline
animal.lifespan: 10–12 years in the wild; to ~20 in captivity
animal.size: 22–55 kg; body 0.9–1.3 m with a tail 0.8–1 m
animal.behaviour: Unlike other big cats it cannot roar; it chuffs, mews and wails instead. It wraps its tail over its nose and face for warmth while sleeping.
fieldMarks: Smoky-grey to cream fur with dark open rosettes
Short muzzle and pale green or grey eyes
animal.voice: Cannot roar; makes yowls, moans and a puffing 'chuff'
animal.lookalikes: Common leopard is golden with denser rosettes and a shorter, thinner tail, and lives mostly at lower elevations.
animal.whereToSee: Hemis National Park (Ladakh) and the Spiti Valley around Kibber, India, with local trackers
animal.season: Resident; winter (Jan–Mar) brings cats lower and is the usual tracking season

lore: The winged snow leopard Aq Bars appears on the coat of arms of Tatarstan, and the snow leopard is an emblem of Almaty and of Kyrgyzstan. Peter Matthiessen's 1978 book The Snow Leopard made the cat a Western symbol of the unseen.
funFact: Its tail can be nearly as long as its body, the longest relative to body size of any big cat.

summary: The largest wild member of the dog family and the ancestor of every domestic dog. Wolves live in family packs that cooperate to hunt animals far larger than themselves across the Northern Hemisphere.
nativeRange: North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa's edge; extirpated from much of its former range and returning in parts of Europe and the US
abilities: Hunts cooperatively in packs to bring down elk, moose and bison
Howls that carry for kilometres and help scattered pack members regroup
Can travel tens of kilometres in a day at a steady trot
As an apex predator, shifts the behaviour and numbers of prey, with knock-on effects on vegetation

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, elk, moose, caribou, bison, smaller mammals; scavenges carrion
animal.habitat: Almost any habitat with enough prey, from Arctic tundra to desert
animal.lifespan: 6–8 years typical in the wild; up to ~13; longer in captivity
animal.size: 25–80 kg; head-body 1–1.6 m
animal.behaviour: A typical pack is a breeding pair and their offspring from the past few years. Young wolves leave to find mates and found new packs, sometimes travelling hundreds of kilometres.
fieldMarks: Usually grizzled grey, but can be white, black or tawny
Broad head and short, rounded ears
Tail carried low; long straight-line trotting gait
animal.voice: A long, low howl, often joined by the pack in chorus
animal.lookalikes: Coyote is much smaller with a narrow, pointed muzzle and larger, pointed ears. Large domestic dogs can look similar; wolves have longer legs and narrow chests. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Lamar Valley, Yellowstone; Algonquin Provincial Park (public howls in late summer)
animal.season: Resident; Yellowstone sightings best in winter and spring

lore: Rome's founding legend tells of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, cast in the bronze Capitoline Wolf. Turkic tradition traces the Ashina dynasty to the she-wolf Asena, and Norse myth gives the end of the world to the wolf Fenrir.
funFact: The 1995–96 reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone changed how elk used the park, a famous case study of how one predator can reshape an ecosystem.

summary: The largest animal known to have ever lived, larger than any dinosaur, reaching about 30 m and well over 150 tonnes. It grows that large almost entirely on krill, shrimp-like animals a few centimetres long.
nativeRange: All oceans except the high Arctic; distinct populations in the North Atlantic, North Pacific, Indian Ocean and Southern Ocean
abilities: Lunge-feeds by engulfing a mouthful of water larger than its own body, then strains it through baleen
Can eat up to around 16 tonnes of krill in a day during the feeding season
Produces low-frequency calls of up to ~188 dB that can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater
Migrates thousands of kilometres between feeding and breeding grounds

animal.diet: Filter feeder: almost entirely krill
animal.habitat: Open ocean and productive upwelling zones along shelf edges
animal.size: Typically 24–27 m; record ~30 m; up to ~150–190 t
animal.behaviour: A lunge takes about ten seconds, the throat pleats ballooning to hold tens of tonnes of water. Calves drink a fat-rich milk and gain around 90 kg a day.
fieldMarks: Tall, straight blow up to about 9 m
Tiny dorsal fin set far back
Broad, U-shaped head; often raises the tail flukes when diving deep
animal.voice: Very loud, low-frequency moans and pulses, mostly below human hearing
animal.lookalikes: Fin whale is darker grey with a taller dorsal fin and an asymmetric jaw (white on the right side). Sei whale is smaller with a more prominent fin.
animal.whereToSee: Mirissa (Sri Lanka), Monterey Bay and the Santa Barbara Channel (California), Loreto in the Gulf of California
animal.season: Sri Lanka Dec–Apr; California Jun–Oct; Gulf of California Feb–Apr

lore: Robert Sibbald described a blue whale stranded on the Firth of Forth in 1692 in his Phalainologia Nova (1694), and the species was long called 'Sibbald's rorqual'. Twentieth-century whaling killed about 360,000 in the Southern Hemisphere before a 1966 ban.
funFact: Its heart weighs about 180 kg, and its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant.

summary: The largest dolphin and the ocean's top predator, found in every ocean from the polar ice to the tropics. Orca populations have distinct diets, hunting methods and call dialects passed down through family lines, which biologists describe as culture.
nativeRange: All oceans; most abundant in cold, productive waters of the North Pacific, North Atlantic and Southern Ocean
abilities: Hunts with echolocation and coordinated group tactics
Creates waves in unison to wash seals off Antarctic ice floes
Deliberately beaches itself to snatch sea lion pups, then wriggles back into the sea (Patagonia, Crozet Islands)
Passes learned dialects and hunting traditions from mothers and grandmothers to offspring
Kills great white sharks and blue whales

animal.diet: Carnivore; varies by population: salmon, herring, seals, sea lions, sharks, other whales
animal.habitat: Coastal and open ocean, especially cold waters
animal.size: Males 6–8 m (rarely ~9 m), up to ~6 t; dorsal fin to 1.8 m
animal.behaviour: Resident orcas of the Pacific Northwest stay with their mothers for life. Females live decades past menopause, and these grandmothers lead the family to salmon in lean years.
fieldMarks: Bold black and white pattern with a white eye patch
Grey 'saddle patch' behind the dorsal fin
Males have a very tall, straight dorsal fin
animal.voice: Clicks, whistles and pulsed calls; each pod has its own dialect
animal.lookalikes: False killer whale is all-dark and slimmer. Risso's dolphin is grey and scarred. Female orcas have curved fins like large dolphins.
animal.whereToSee: San Juan Islands and Salish Sea (Washington/British Columbia); northern Norway (Skjervøy area) in winter; Península Valdés, Argentina
animal.season: Salish Sea mainly summer; Norway Nov–Jan with the herring; Valdés beach-hunting Mar–Apr

lore: Orcas are crest animals of Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast nations, carved on totem poles. At Eden, New South Wales, a pod led by 'Old Tom' herded baleen whales towards human whalers in exchange for the tongues and lips, a partnership that lasted into the 1920s.
funFact: IUCN lists the orca as Data Deficient because it may comprise several species that have not yet been formally separated.

summary: A widespread dolphin of warm and temperate seas, one of the most studied animals for intelligence. Each dolphin develops its own signature whistle, which others use to call it, much like a name.
nativeRange: Temperate and tropical oceans worldwide, coastal and offshore
abilities: Echolocates with clicks precise enough to tell objects apart by shape and material
Uses a signature whistle as a personal name and copies others' whistles to address them
Recognises itself in a mirror
Sleeps with one brain hemisphere at a time, keeping one eye open
Some Florida dolphins herd fish with a ring of stirred-up mud and catch them as they leap out

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, squid, crustaceans
animal.habitat: Bays, estuaries, coasts and offshore waters
animal.behaviour: In Laguna, Brazil, bottlenose dolphins drive mullet towards fishermen and give a signal for when to cast their nets, a cooperation passed down through generations of both dolphins and people.
fieldMarks: Robust grey dolphin, darker on the back
Short, stubby beak and a crease above it
Tall, curved dorsal fin in mid-back
animal.voice: Clicks for echolocation and individual 'signature whistles'
animal.lookalikes: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin is smaller with a longer beak and often belly spots. Common dolphins have an hourglass pattern on the side.
animal.whereToSee: Chanonry Point (Moray Firth) and Cardigan Bay, UK; Sarasota Bay, Florida
animal.season: Resident in many coastal areas; Chanonry best on a rising tide in summer

lore: Herodotus tells how a dolphin carried the singer Arion of Lesbos to shore. Pliny the Younger described a dolphin at Hippo (in modern Tunisia) that befriended a boy and let him ride on its back.
funFact: Dolphins remember the signature whistles of former companions after more than 20 years apart.

summary: One of the smallest marine mammals, and unlike most it has no blubber, keeping warm instead with the densest fur of any animal. By eating sea urchins, sea otters protect kelp forests, a textbook case of a keystone species.
nativeRange: Coastal North Pacific, from Hokkaido and the Kuril Islands through Alaska to California
abilities: Floats on its back and cracks shellfish against a stone balanced on its chest
Keeps a favourite stone in a loose pouch of skin under its forearm
Has fur of up to ~150,000 hairs per square centimetre, which traps an insulating layer of air
Controls urchin numbers, allowing kelp forests to grow and support many other species

animal.diet: Carnivore: sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails; eats about a quarter of its body weight daily
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, often within 1–2 km of shore
animal.size: 1–1.5 m; males 22–45 kg, females 14–33 kg
animal.behaviour: Rafts of resting otters wrap themselves in kelp or hold paws so they don't drift apart. Mothers float their pups on their bellies.
fieldMarks: Large otter floating on its back
Dense brown fur, paler grizzled head
Small ears, blunt face, flipper-like hind feet
Uses rocks as tools on its chest
animal.voice: Squeals and whistles, especially from pups
animal.lookalikes: Harbour seals lie belly-down and lack visible paws. River otters swim on their bellies with long, tapering tails.
animal.whereToSee: Monterey Bay and Elkhorn Slough (California); Kenai Fjords and Prince William Sound (Alaska)

lore: After Vitus Bering's 1741 expedition returned with pelts, Russian and later British and American traders sold sea otter fur to China, nearly wiping the species out. The 1911 Fur Seal Treaty ended the hunt when perhaps 1,000–2,000 remained.
funFact: Sea otters are among the few mammals other than primates known to use stone tools.

summary: North America's largest rodent and one of its most important ecosystem engineers. Beaver dams turn streams into ponds and wetlands that store water, trap sediment and shelter fish, amphibians and birds.
nativeRange: Most of North America from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico; introduced to Tierra del Fuego and Finland
abilities: Fells trees with self-sharpening incisors whose front enamel is strengthened with iron, giving it an orange colour
Builds dams of logs, mud and stone and repairs leaks it hears or feels flowing
Stays underwater for up to ~15 minutes, with ears and nostrils that close and clear membranes over the eyes
Creates wetlands that raise water tables and act as firebreaks during wildfires

animal.diet: Herbivore: bark, cambium, twigs and leaves of willow, aspen and other trees; aquatic plants
animal.habitat: Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes bordered by trees
animal.size: 11–32 kg; 0.9–1.2 m including the flat tail
animal.behaviour: Families live in a domed lodge with underwater entrances and store branches in the pond mud as a winter food cache. A tail slap on the water warns the colony of danger.
fieldMarks: Large brown rodent with a flat, scaly, paddle-shaped tail
Swims low with only the head showing
Dams, lodges and gnawed tree stumps nearby
animal.voice: Slaps its tail loudly on the water when alarmed
animal.lookalikes: Muskrat is much smaller with a thin tail. Nutria has white whiskers and a round, rat-like tail. Otters swim with a long tapering tail.
animal.whereToSee: Algonquin Provincial Park (Ontario); Grand Teton and Rocky Mountain national parks
animal.season: Resident; most active at dawn and dusk

uses.use: Castoreum, the scent-gland secretion of beavers, was prescribed for headaches, fevers and 'hysteria'
Castoreum used in remedies for pain and as a scent lure

compounds: salicylic acid derivatives (from willow bark in the diet)
medicinal.cautions: Historical use only; castoreum is not a recognised modern medicine.

lore: Demand for beaver-felt hats drove the fur trade that mapped much of Canada; the Hudson's Bay Company (1670) priced goods in 'made beaver' pelts. In Anishinaabe tradition, Amik is among the animals that dive to bring up mud to make the world.
funFact: A beaver dam in Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada, is about 850 m long and can be seen in satellite images.

summary: A black-and-white bear of the cool bamboo forests of central China that lives almost entirely on bamboo, despite having the gut of a carnivore. Decades of reserve-building helped wild numbers recover to about 1,860 adults.
nativeRange: Mountains of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu provinces, China
abilities: Grips bamboo with a 'pseudo-thumb', an enlarged wrist bone that works like a sixth digit
Eats 12–38 kg of bamboo a day and spends 10–16 hours feeding
Survives on a low-energy diet by keeping its metabolism unusually low for its size
Crushes tough bamboo stems with massive jaw muscles and broad molars

animal.diet: Herbivore in practice (~99% bamboo); occasionally carrion or small animals
animal.habitat: Temperate montane forests with dense bamboo understorey, 1,200–3,400 m
animal.behaviour: Newborns weigh 90–130 g, about 1/900th of their mother, among the smallest newborns relative to the mother of any placental mammal.
fieldMarks: Black eye patches, ears, legs and shoulder band
Round face with heavy cheek muscles
Often seen sitting and eating bamboo
animal.voice: Bleats, huffs, honks and barks
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Wild pandas are very rarely seen; Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding and Wolong reserve's centres in Sichuan

lore: The French missionary-naturalist Armand David sent the first panda skin to Paris in 1869. Since the 1950s China has lent pandas to other nations as diplomatic gifts, a practice called 'panda diplomacy'.
funFact: IUCN downgraded the giant panda from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016 as its wild population grew.

summary: A russet, ring-tailed tree-dweller of the eastern Himalaya, the only living member of its family and not a close relative of the giant panda. It was called 'panda' first, decades before the giant panda was known to Western science.
nativeRange: Nepal, Bhutan, northeast India, Myanmar and southwest China
abilities: Has a false thumb (an extended wrist bone) for gripping bamboo, evolved separately from the giant panda's
Climbs down trees head-first by rotating its ankles
Lowers its metabolic rate and curls its thick tail around itself to save energy in the cold
Detects sweetness with taste receptors for artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, unusual among mammals

animal.diet: Mostly bamboo leaves and shoots; also fruit, acorns, eggs and insects
animal.habitat: Temperate forest with bamboo understorey, 2,200–4,800 m
animal.lifespan: 8–10 years wild; up to ~15 in captivity
animal.size: 3–6 kg; body 50–64 cm with a tail of 28–59 cm
animal.behaviour: Mostly solitary and active at dawn, dusk and night, it sleeps stretched along branches by day.
fieldMarks: White face markings and tear-like stripes
animal.voice: Twittering whistles and huff-quacks
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable in its range.
animal.whereToSee: Singalila National Park, Darjeeling (India)
animal.season: Resident; easiest about Mar–May and Oct–Dec

lore: Frédéric Cuvier named it Ailurus fulgens, 'shining cat', in 1825. The word 'panda' probably comes from a Nepali name for the animal.
funFact: The Firefox web browser is named after it, from a Chinese name meaning 'fire fox'.

summary: A red-haired great ape of northern Sumatra's rainforests, the most tree-bound of all great apes. Mothers raise each infant for about eight to nine years, and young orangutans learn which plants to eat and which tools to make by watching them.
nativeRange: Northern Sumatra, Indonesia (mainly Aceh and North Sumatra, including the Leuser Ecosystem)
abilities: Uses sticks to pry nutritious seeds from spiny Neesia fruits without touching the irritating hairs
Builds a fresh sleeping nest of folded branches high in the canopy every night
A wild male, Rakus, was observed in 2022 chewing a medicinal liana and applying it to a facial wound, which then healed
Disperses the seeds of many rainforest trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit (especially figs), plus leaves, bark, insects; occasionally slow lorises
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest and peat swamp forest
animal.size: Males 70–90 kg, ~1.4 m tall standing, arm span over 2 m; females ~35–45 kg
animal.behaviour: Adult males develop broad cheek pads and give 'long calls' that carry about a kilometre through the forest. Births come about every 8–9 years, the longest interval of any mammal.
fieldMarks: Large ape with long, pale reddish-orange hair
Adult males develop broad cheek pads and a beard
animal.voice: Flanged males give a loud, booming 'long call'
animal.lookalikes: Bornean orangutans are darker red with shorter hair; Tapanuli orangutans live in a small area of North Sumatra and have frizzier hair.
animal.whereToSee: Bukit Lawang and Ketambe in Gunung Leuser National Park, Sumatra, with licensed guides

lore: The Dutch physician Jacobus Bontius described an 'Orang Outang' from the East Indies in 1658, and Linnaeus drew on such reports for his 'Homo troglodytes'. Sumatran orangutans were recognised as a species separate from Bornean ones in the late 20th century.
funFact: Rakus's wound treatment was the first systematically documented case of a wild animal treating its own wound with a plant known to contain medically active substances.

summary: Along with the bonobo, the chimpanzee is humanity's closest living relative, sharing about 98–99% of our DNA. Different chimp communities have their own traditions of tool use, grooming and hunting, passed on by learning.
nativeRange: Equatorial Africa from Senegal and Guinea to Uganda and western Tanzania
abilities: Strips twigs into probes to fish termites from mounds
Cracks hard nuts with stone or wooden hammers on anvils, a practice dated to at least 4,300 years ago in Côte d'Ivoire
At Fongoli, Senegal, sharpens sticks into spears to stab bushbabies in tree hollows
Hunts colobus monkeys cooperatively and shares the meat
Swallows rough leaves whole and chews bitter pith, behaviours linked to fighting parasites

animal.diet: Omnivore: mainly ripe fruit, plus leaves, seeds, insects, honey and meat
animal.habitat: Rainforest, swamp forest and savanna woodland
animal.lifespan: 40–50 years in the wild; 60+ in captivity
animal.size: Males 40–70 kg, females 27–50 kg; ~1–1.7 m standing
animal.behaviour: Communities split into shifting subgroups by day and patrol their borders. Males form alliances, and violent conflicts between communities have been recorded.
fieldMarks: Ape with black hair and bare face, hands and feet
animal.voice: Loud 'pant-hoots' that rise to a scream; drums on tree buttresses
animal.lookalikes: Bonobo is slimmer with a smaller head, pink lips and hair parted in the middle; it lives only south of the Congo River.
animal.whereToSee: Gombe and Mahale (Tanzania), Kibale (Uganda), with permit-led tracking groups

lore: Edward Tyson's 1699 anatomy of a 'Pygmie', titled Orang-Outang, sive Homo Sylvestris, was in fact a young chimpanzee and was the first scientific dissection of an ape. In 1960 Jane Goodall saw the Gombe chimpanzee David Greybeard fish for termites, overturning the idea that only humans make tools.
funFact: Chimpanzees outperform human students on some quick short-term memory tests for numbers flashed on a screen.

summary: The largest living primate, a mostly gentle, plant-eating ape of the Congo Basin and Nigeria–Cameroon forests. Families centre on a silverback male who leads, mediates and protects the group.
nativeRange: Western equatorial Africa: Cameroon, Gabon, Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Angola (Cabinda); Cross River gorillas on the Nigeria–Cameroon border
abilities: Beats its chest with cupped hands, a sound that can carry about 1 km; in mountain gorillas, the pitch of the beats has been shown to signal the male's body size
Wild western gorillas have been seen testing water depth with a walking stick
Captive gorillas such as Koko learned hundreds of signs
Disperses large seeds of many forest trees

animal.diet: Herbivore: fruit, leaves, stems, pith; also termites and ants
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest and swamp clearings (bais)
animal.size: Males 140–200 kg and up to ~1.7 m standing; females 70–100 kg
animal.behaviour: Each evening every gorilla builds a nest of leaves and branches on the ground or in a tree. Western gorillas travel further each day than mountain gorillas, following fruiting trees.
fieldMarks: Very large ape with dark grey-brown hair
Adult males have a silver back and a crest on the head
Lives in groups led by a silverback
animal.voice: Chest-beating, hoots and grunts
animal.lookalikes: Eastern gorillas (mountain and Grauer's) are darker and longer-haired and live far to the east.
animal.whereToSee: Odzala-Kokoua (Republic of Congo), Dzanga-Sangha (Central African Republic) and Loango (Gabon), with habituated-group permits

lore: The Carthaginian Hanno's Periplus (c. 5th century BCE) tells of hairy wild people on a West African island that interpreters called 'Gorillai'. Thomas Savage and Jeffries Wyman described the gorilla for science in 1847 and borrowed that name.
funFact: Gorillas hum and 'sing' while they eat, especially when the food is good.

summary: The most widespread three-toed sloth, a leaf-eater that saves energy by moving very little and very slowly. Its shaggy fur carries algae, moths and fungi, a small ecosystem of its own.
nativeRange: Honduras south through Central America to northern Argentina, east of the Andes
abilities: Has 8–9 neck vertebrae instead of the usual seven, letting it turn its head about 270°
Slows its heart and can stay underwater for many minutes; a good swimmer
Hangs effortlessly thanks to locking tendons in its curved claws
Grows green algae in grooved hairs that camouflage it among leaves

animal.diet: Folivore: leaves of Cecropia and many other trees
animal.habitat: Lowland and montane rainforest canopy
animal.behaviour: About once a week it climbs to the ground to defecate, its most dangerous trip. Moths living in its fur lay eggs in the dung, and their offspring fly back up to colonise the sloth.
fieldMarks: Shaggy grey-brown fur, often greenish with algae
Brown throat and dark eye stripe
Three long curved claws on each forelimb
Males have an orange-and-black back patch
animal.voice: A high, whistled 'ai-ai'
animal.lookalikes: Two-toed sloths (Choloepus) have two front claws, a pinkish snout and no eye mask.
animal.whereToSee: Manuel Antonio and Cahuita national parks, Costa Rica

lore: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, in his 1526 natural history of the Indies, called the sloth the most useless and ugliest animal he had seen and recorded its local name, perico ligero.
funFact: A meal can take up to a month to pass through a sloth's chambered stomach.

summary: A scaly, toothless ant-eater of Southeast Asian forests and plantations, armoured in overlapping keratin scales. Pangolins are thought to be the most trafficked wild mammals, poached for meat and scales.
nativeRange: Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra, Java, Borneo and nearby islands
abilities: Rolls into a tight, armoured ball that most predators cannot open
Rips into ant and termite nests with powerful foreclaws
Catches insects with a long, sticky tongue anchored deep in the chest
Seals its nostrils and ears against biting ants while feeding
Grinds food with swallowed stones and keratin spines in its stomach instead of teeth

animal.diet: Insectivore: ants and termites, including eggs and larvae
animal.habitat: Primary and secondary forest, plantations, gardens
animal.lifespan: Unknown in the wild; ~20 years recorded in captivity for pangolins
animal.size: Body 40–65 cm plus a similar tail; ~4–10 kg
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal, it climbs well with its prehensile tail and sleeps in tree hollows or burrows. Mothers carry their single young on the base of the tail.
fieldMarks: Small head and long tail used for gripping
Rolls into a ball when threatened
animal.lookalikes: Chinese pangolin has larger ears and a shorter tail; Philippine pangolin lives only in Palawan.

lore: The English word comes from Malay pengguling, 'one that rolls up'. Pangolin scales have long been used in traditional Chinese medicine; in 2020 China removed them from its official pharmacopoeia and gave pangolins top legal protection.
funFact: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, the same protein as human fingernails.

summary: An egg-laying, duck-billed mammal of eastern Australia's rivers and one of only five living monotremes. It hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut, finding prey by the electrical fields of their muscles.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia and Tasmania; introduced to Kangaroo Island
abilities: Detects the electrical fields of moving prey with about 40,000 electroreceptors in its bill
Males deliver a venom from hind-leg spurs that causes intense, lasting pain in humans
Lays leathery eggs and feeds young on milk sweated from patches of skin, as it has no nipples
Its fur glows blue-green under ultraviolet light
Stores food in cheek pouches and grinds it with horny pads instead of teeth

animal.diet: Carnivore: insect larvae, freshwater shrimp, yabbies, worms
animal.habitat: Freshwater streams, rivers and lakes with earth banks for burrows
animal.lifespan: Up to ~21 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Females dig long nesting burrows and plug them with soil to guard their eggs. Platypuses eat around a fifth of their body weight in a day.
fieldMarks: Small brown furry mammal with a soft duck-like bill
Dives briefly, leaving rings on the water
animal.lookalikes: Australian water-rat (rakali) has a white-tipped tail and a rat-like head. Males have a venomous spur on each hind ankle; never handle one.
animal.whereToSee: Broken River, Eungella National Park and the Atherton Tablelands (Queensland); Tasmania's rivers
animal.season: Resident; best at dawn and dusk

lore: When a dried specimen reached the British zoologist George Shaw in 1799, he suspected a hoax and looked for stitches joining a duck's bill to a mammal's body. In Aboriginal stories from New South Wales the platypus is the child of a duck and a water-rat.
funFact: The platypus has no stomach: its gullet connects directly to its intestine.

otherNames: Kǎolā 考拉 / Shùdàixióng 树袋熊 (Chinese)
summary: A tree-dwelling marsupial that lives almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in energy and toxic to most animals. Koalas sleep or rest for up to 20 hours a day to save energy.
nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern Australia (Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia)
abilities: Detoxifies eucalyptus oils with liver enzymes and gut microbes
Ferments leaves in a caecum up to ~2 m long, the longest relative to body size of any mammal
Males bellow at a very low pitch using a pair of extra vocal folds above the larynx
Has fingerprints that closely resemble human ones

animal.diet: Eucalyptus leaves, from a few dozen preferred species; little need to drink
animal.habitat: Eucalyptus forests and woodlands
animal.size: 4–15 kg (southern koalas larger); 60–85 cm
animal.behaviour: Mothers feed joeys a special soft dropping called 'pap', which passes on the gut microbes needed to digest eucalyptus.
fieldMarks: Stocky grey marsupial with a big black nose
Sits in eucalyptus forks, often asleep
animal.voice: Males give loud, deep snoring bellows, mostly in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Great Otway National Park (Kennett River) and Phillip Island's Koala Conservation Reserve (Victoria); Magnetic Island (Queensland)

lore: The name is usually traced to Dharug gula. Millions of koalas were killed for fur in the early 20th century; public outrage at Queensland's 1927 open season led the Commonwealth to stop issuing export permits for koala skins, effectively ending the trade.
funFact: The koala is not a bear; its closest living relatives are wombats.

summary: The largest living marsupial, a long-legged hopper of Australia's dry interior. Hopping is so efficient at speed that a kangaroo uses little more energy going faster.
nativeRange: Arid and semi-arid mainland Australia
abilities: Bounds at up to ~60 km/h and covers 8 m or more in a single leap
Stores and returns energy in its elastic leg tendons like a spring
Uses its muscular tail as a fifth leg when moving slowly
Can pause the development of an embryo (embryonic diapause) until conditions improve
Can have an embryo, a joey in the pouch and a joey at foot at the same time, producing two kinds of milk from different teats

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses and forbs; can go long periods without drinking
animal.habitat: Open plains, desert and shrubland with scattered shade trees
animal.lifespan: Up to ~20 years; often less in the wild
animal.size: Males up to ~85 kg and ~1.6 m long plus tail; females ~35 kg
animal.behaviour: Rival males 'box', grappling with forearms and kicking with their hind feet while balanced on their tails. Kangaroos lick their forearms to cool off.
fieldMarks: Black and white marks on the muzzle
animal.lookalikes: Eastern and western grey kangaroos lack the black and white muzzle marks and have dark tail tips. Large males can kick and box. Keep a respectful distance.
animal.whereToSee: Sturt National Park (NSW), Flinders Ranges (SA) and Mutawintji National Park
animal.season: Resident; active at dawn and dusk

lore: Joseph Banks and James Cook recorded the word 'kangaroo' from Guugu Yimithirr speakers at the Endeavour River in 1770 (their animal was a grey kangaroo). The red kangaroo appears on Australia's coat of arms.
funFact: Females are often blue-grey while males are red, which is why females are nicknamed 'blue fliers'.

summary: One of the largest bats in the world, with a wingspan up to about 1.5 m. These fruit- and nectar-eating bats fly long distances each night, spreading pollen and seeds across Southeast Asian forests.
nativeRange: Southeast Asia: mainland from southern Myanmar and Vietnam to Malaysia, plus Sumatra, Java, Borneo, the Philippines and Lesser Sundas
abilities: Flies 50 km or more in a night between roosts and feeding trees
Pollinates night-flowering trees and disperses seeds over long distances
Finds food by sight and smell rather than echolocation
Hangs upside down using tendons that lock its claws without effort

animal.diet: Frugivore and nectarivore: fruit, nectar and flowers
animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and orchards; roosts in large colonies in tall trees
animal.lifespan: ~15 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: 0.6–1.1 kg; wingspan up to ~1.5 m
animal.behaviour: Colonies of hundreds to thousands roost in the same trees by day and fan out at dusk, often crossing open sea between islands.
fieldMarks: Huge fruit bat with a wingspan up to about 1.5 m
Black wings and reddish or brown mantle
animal.voice: Loud squabbling and shrieks at roosts
animal.lookalikes: Golden-crowned flying fox (Philippines) has a golden head. Flying foxes can carry viruses; never handle bats.
animal.whereToSee: Subic Bay Forest Reserve roost (Philippines)

lore: Linnaeus named it Vespertilio vampyrus in 1758, linking it to vampire legends, though it eats only fruit and nectar. In Malaysia it has long been hunted for food and as a folk remedy for asthma.
funFact: Flying foxes like this one are natural hosts of Nipah virus, which they carry without getting sick.

summary: A nearly hairless, buck-toothed rodent that lives underground in East Africa in colonies run like an insect hive, with a single breeding queen. It is also extraordinarily long-lived and resistant to cancer, making it a major subject of ageing research.
nativeRange: Arid grasslands of Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya
abilities: Lives more than 37 years, about ten times longer than a similar-sized mouse
Survives about 18 minutes without oxygen by switching to fructose-based metabolism
Very rarely develops cancer
Feels no pain from acid or from capsaicin, the burning compound in chilli
Digs tunnels with its large front teeth, which sit outside its lips so it can dig without swallowing soil

animal.diet: Herbivore: large underground tubers and roots
animal.habitat: Underground tunnel systems up to several kilometres long in hard, dry soil
animal.size: 8–10 cm; 30–35 g (queens larger)
animal.behaviour: A colony of up to ~300 has one queen and a few breeding males; the rest are workers and soldiers. Each colony has its own dialect of chirps.
animal.voice: Chirps and squeaks; a rich vocal repertoire
animal.season: Resident; almost never seen above ground

lore: Eduard Rüppell described the species in 1842. In 1981 Jennifer Jarvis showed that it is eusocial, the first mammal shown to live like social insects.
funFact: Unlike most mammals, it can barely regulate its own body temperature, so colonies huddle together or move to warmer tunnels.

summary: A salamander that never grows up: it keeps its feathery gills and lives its whole life in water. It can regrow lost limbs, parts of its spinal cord, heart and brain, and is a major subject of regeneration research. In the wild it survives only in the canals of Xochimilco in Mexico City.
nativeRange: Lake Xochimilco (and formerly Lake Chalco), Valley of Mexico
abilities: Regrows complete limbs, tail, parts of the heart, spinal cord, eyes and brain without scarring
Keeps juvenile features such as external gills into adulthood and breeds that way (neoteny)
Breathes through gills, skin and simple lungs
Accepts transplanted organs from other axolotls with little rejection

animal.diet: Carnivore: worms, insect larvae, crustaceans, small fish
animal.habitat: Cool, high-altitude lake and canal water with dense vegetation
animal.size: Usually 15–30 cm; up to ~45 cm
animal.behaviour: Wild axolotls are dark mottled brown; the pink and white forms common in aquariums come from captive breeding lines.
fieldMarks: Stays aquatic with feathery external gills
Wild form brown to dark grey with gold speckles
Long tail fin running from the head
animal.lookalikes: Larvae of tiger salamanders and other neotenic mole salamanders look very similar. Mudpuppies (Necturus) are also confused with axolotls.
animal.whereToSee: Wild animals are very rarely seen in the canals of Xochimilco, Mexico City; widely shown in zoos and aquariums

lore: Named for the Aztec god Xolotl, who in legend turned himself into an axolotl to escape being sacrificed. Axolotls were eaten in the Aztec period and the 16th-century Florentine Codex records them as food.
funFact: A 2014 survey found about 36 axolotls per square kilometre in Xochimilco, down from about 6,000 in 1998.

summary: A thumb-sized, brightly patterned frog of the Guiana Shield whose colours warn predators that its skin is laced with alkaloid toxins. Its many colour forms include the electric-blue frogs once treated as a separate species, Dendrobates azureus.
nativeRange: Guiana Shield: French Guiana, Suriname, Guyana and adjacent northern Brazil
abilities: Stores alkaloid toxins such as pumiliotoxins in its skin, taken from the ants and mites it eats
Warns predators with vivid, highly variable colour patterns (aposematism)
Males carry newly hatched tadpoles on their backs to small pools of water in tree holes or bromeliads
Captive-bred frogs fed on other insects lose their toxicity

animal.diet: Small invertebrates: ants, mites, termites, small beetles
animal.habitat: Humid forest floor near streams, boulders and fallen trees
animal.behaviour: Females compete for males and may wrestle rivals. Toxic species like this one are active by day, relying on their warning colours rather than hiding.
fieldMarks: Small frog with bright, highly variable colours
Often black with yellow or white stripes
animal.voice: Quiet, buzzing calls
animal.lookalikes: Other dendrobatids are similar; colour morphs vary between populations. Its skin toxins can harm — do not touch.
animal.whereToSee: Brownsberg Nature Park (Suriname)

lore: Its name comes from tapirage, an Amazonian practice reported by European travellers: rubbing a frog's secretions onto plucked parrot skin was said to make the new feathers grow yellow or red. Unlike some relatives, this species was not the main source of dart poisons.
funFact: The blue 'Okopipi' frogs of Suriname's Sipaliwini savanna were described as their own species in 1969 but are now considered a colour form of this one.

summary: The world's largest living lizard, found on only a handful of Indonesian islands. It ambushes deer, pigs and water buffalo, and its bite delivers a venom that stops blood clotting.
nativeRange: Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Motang and Nusa Kode (Gili Dasami), Lesser Sunda Islands, Indonesia
abilities: Has venom glands in its lower jaw that release anticoagulant toxins and cause shock
Picks up the scent of carrion from several kilometres away with its forked tongue
Females can reproduce without males (parthenogenesis), as two zoo dragons did in 2006
Can eat up to 80% of its body weight in one meal
Its serrated teeth have iron-rich orange tips that resist wear

animal.diet: Carnivore: deer, pigs, water buffalo, carrion; young eat insects and geckos
animal.habitat: Hot, dry lowland savanna and monsoon forest
animal.size: Males up to ~3 m and 70–90 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Young dragons live in trees to avoid being eaten by adults and roll in dung to make themselves less appealing.
fieldMarks: Young are greenish with yellow-black bands and live in trees
animal.lookalikes: Water monitors are smaller with yellow patterned skin; any large monitor here may be a Komodo. Never approach on foot; visits require park rangers.
animal.whereToSee: Loh Liang (Komodo Island) and Loh Buaya (Rinca), Komodo National Park — ranger-led walks only
animal.season: Resident; dry season (about Apr–Dec) is the usual visiting season

lore: On Komodo, villagers tell of a princess who gave birth to twins, a human boy and a dragon, Ora, so people and dragons are kin. Western science learned of it in 1910 through Dutch officer J.K.H. van Steyn van Hensbroek, and Peter Ouwens named it in 1912.
funFact: IUCN moved the Komodo dragon to Endangered in 2021, partly because rising seas are expected to shrink its small island habitat.

summary: A large sea turtle of tropical and subtropical seas, named for the greenish fat under its shell. Adults are the only sea turtles that graze mainly on seagrass and algae, keeping seagrass meadows healthy.
nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide; nests on beaches in over 80 countries
abilities: Navigates thousands of kilometres using Earth's magnetic field and returns to nest near the beach where it hatched
Swims about 2,000 km from Brazil to nest on tiny Ascension Island
Mows seagrass beds, which keeps the meadows productive
Can rest underwater for hours by slowing its heart

animal.diet: Juveniles omnivorous; adults herbivorous: seagrass and algae
animal.habitat: Coastal seagrass and reef feeding grounds; open ocean as juveniles; sandy beaches for nesting
animal.size: Shell 0.8–1.2 m (to ~1.5 m); usually 110–190 kg
animal.behaviour: Females crawl ashore at night every few years to dig nests, laying around 100 eggs several times a season. Nest temperature decides hatchlings' sex: warmer sand produces more females.
fieldMarks: Large sea turtle with a smooth, heart-shaped shell
Small, rounded head with one pair of scales between the eyes
animal.lookalikes: Hawksbill has a pointed, hawk-like beak and overlapping shell plates. Loggerhead has a large head and reddish-brown shell.
animal.whereToSee: Tortuguero (Costa Rica), Ras al Jinz (Oman) and Heron Island (Great Barrier Reef), with guided night viewing
animal.season: Tortuguero nesting Jul–Oct; Ras al Jinz all year, peak Jun–Sep; Heron Island Nov–Mar

lore: In Hawaiian tradition the honu is an ʻaumakua (family guardian), and the turtle Kauila was said to take the form of a girl to watch over children at Punaluʻu. Green turtle soup was a showpiece of London's Lord Mayor's banquets from the 18th century, driving heavy Caribbean harvests.
funFact: In October 2025 the IUCN moved the green turtle from Endangered to Least Concern after decades of protecting nesting beaches, though some regional populations remain threatened.

otherNames: Jiālāpàgēsī xiàngguī 加拉帕戈斯象龟 (Chinese)
summary: The largest living tortoise, gave the Galápagos Islands their name. Different islands have different forms, with domed shells in wet highlands and raised 'saddleback' shells on dry islands, which helped shape Darwin's thinking. The IUCN assesses each island species separately, from Vulnerable to Critically Endangered; strictly, the name Chelonoidis niger now belongs to the Floreana tortoise, which is extinct.
nativeRange: Galápagos Islands, Ecuador (Isabela, Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal, Española, Pinzón, Santiago and others)
abilities: Lives well over 100 years
Survives up to a year without food or water by storing water and fat
Saddleback forms raise their necks high to reach cactus pads
Spreads seeds and tramples paths, shaping Galápagos plant communities

animal.diet: Herbivore: grasses, leaves, cactus pads, fruit and lichens
animal.habitat: Dry lowlands to humid highlands of volcanic islands
animal.size: Up to ~1.5 m shell length and over 400 kg
animal.behaviour: Tortoises migrate seasonally between lowlands and highlands, wearing paths used for centuries. Small finches hop in front of them, and tortoises stretch up their necks so the birds can pick off ticks.
fieldMarks: Shell domed or saddle-backed depending on island
Long neck and heavy, elephant-like legs
Wallows in pools in the highlands
animal.voice: Males make loud, rhythmic groans during mating
animal.lookalikes: The different islands' tortoises are now treated as several species; shell shape and island tell them apart.
animal.whereToSee: El Chato and Rancho Primicias reserves on Santa Cruz island; the Charles Darwin Research Station

lore: Spanish sailors named the islands for the galápago, an old word for tortoise. In 1835 the vice-governor told Darwin he could tell which island a tortoise came from by its shell; whalers took more than 100,000 tortoises (some estimates say 200,000) as live food for their voyages.
funFact: IUCN assesses each island form separately, from Vulnerable to Critically Endangered; the Floreana and Pinta forms were wiped out, and Pinta's last tortoise, Lonesome George, died in 2012.

otherNames: Yǎnjìng wáng shé 眼镜王蛇 (Chinese)
summary: The world's longest venomous snake, up to about 5.5 m, and a hunter that eats mainly other snakes. Females are the only snakes known to build nests, piling leaves into a mound and guarding the eggs.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia; since a 2024 revision, Ophiophagus hannah in the narrow sense covers eastern Pakistan, northern and eastern India, the Andaman Islands, Myanmar and Indochina south to central Thailand, with the king cobras of the Western Ghats, the Sunda region and Luzon assigned to related species
abilities: Rears up to about a third of its body length and spreads a narrow hood when threatened
Makes a low growl-like hiss with air pushed through its windpipe
Injects large volumes of neurotoxic venom, enough to kill an elephant
Hunts other snakes, including venomous ones, following their scent

animal.diet: Mostly snakes (rat snakes, pythons, cobras, kraits); occasionally lizards
animal.habitat: Forests, mangroves and plantations near streams
animal.size: Usually 3–4 m; record about 5.5–5.85 m; 6–12 kg
animal.behaviour: Females stay with their nest of 20–40 eggs for weeks, but leave just before hatching, possibly so they won't eat their young.
fieldMarks: Very long, olive to brown snake with pale bands
Large head with big scales on top
Raises the front part of its body and spreads a narrow hood
animal.voice: Can give a low growling hiss
animal.lookalikes: Rat snakes and other large non-venomous snakes look similar; never try to tell them apart up close. Spectacled and monocled cobras are smaller with marked hoods. Never approach on foot; back away and alert local snake rescuers.

lore: Cobras, the nāgas of Hindu and Buddhist tradition, are worshipped on Nag Panchami. In Burma and Thailand, snake charmers perform with king cobras, and in some rituals women kiss the snake's head.
funFact: Its genus name Ophiophagus means 'snake-eater'.

summary: A big, vividly coloured chameleon of northern and eastern Madagascar. Males of each locality have distinct colour patterns, from turquoise to flame-red, and change colour when they display.
nativeRange: Northern and eastern Madagascar and nearby islands; introduced to Réunion and Mauritius
abilities: Changes colour by adjusting the spacing of guanine nanocrystals in its skin, which shifts how light reflects
Fires its tongue out to more than its body length in a fraction of a second
Moves each eye independently, scanning nearly 360°, then focuses both on prey
Grips branches with pincer-like feet and a prehensile tail

animal.diet: Insectivore: crickets, grasshoppers, flies, other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Bushes and trees in warm, humid lowlands, often near villages
animal.size: Males up to ~50 cm including tail; females about half that
animal.behaviour: When a rival male approaches, a male inflates his body and flashes brilliant colour. A female signals refusal with dark colours and orange patches.
fieldMarks: Large chameleon with a bony crest on the head
Males brightly coloured — green, red, blue or orange depending on locality
animal.lookalikes: Other Furcifer and Calumma chameleons; colours vary by region.
animal.whereToSee: Nosy Be (Lokobe), Ankarana and Amber Mountain, northern Madagascar
animal.season: Resident; most visible in the warm, wet season

lore: In many Malagasy communities chameleons are fady (taboo), and touching one is unlucky. Georges Cuvier described the species in 1829.
funFact: A 2015 study on panther chameleons showed that their colour change comes from tuning nanocrystals, not just moving pigments.

summary: The largest living reptile, with old males exceeding 6 m and a tonne. It thrives in fresh and salt water and has crossed open sea to colonise islands from India to the Pacific.
nativeRange: Eastern India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands
abilities: Has the strongest bite measured in any living animal, about 16,000 newtons
Rides ocean currents to travel hundreds of kilometres between coasts
Gets rid of excess salt through glands on its tongue
Can stay submerged for an hour or more while resting
Detects tiny ripples with pressure-sensing pits along its jaws and body

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, crabs, turtles, birds, pigs, buffalo; anything it can overpower
animal.habitat: Tidal rivers, mangrove swamps, estuaries and coasts
animal.size: Males usually 4–5 m, exceptionally 6 m+ and 1,000 kg; females ~3 m
animal.behaviour: Mothers guard their nest mounds, dig out the chirping hatchlings and carry them to water in their mouths. Nest temperature sets the hatchlings' sex.
fieldMarks: Broad snout with ridges running from the eyes
Few or no large scales behind the head
animal.lookalikes: Freshwater crocodile (Australia) is smaller with a narrow snout. Mugger has a broad snout and large neck scales. Any crocodile here may be a saltie. Never approach on foot; keep well back from the water's edge and obey warning signs.
animal.whereToSee: Yellow Water cruises (Kakadu) and the Adelaide River (Northern Territory); Bhitarkanika (Odisha)
animal.season: Resident; dry season best for viewing

lore: A Timorese legend tells that Timor island is the body of a crocodile who befriended a boy. In Arnhem Land the crocodile is an ancestral being of the Dreaming, painted on bark and rock.
funFact: Lolong, captured in the Philippines in 2011, measured 6.17 m, the largest crocodile ever measured in captivity.

summary: The largest predatory fish, a warm-bodied hunter of seals and sea lions in cool coastal seas around the world. Tagging shows these sharks crossing whole ocean basins.
nativeRange: Temperate and subtropical coastal and open waters worldwide; hotspots off South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, California, Guadalupe Island and the north-west Atlantic
abilities: Senses the faint electric fields of living prey with ampullae of Lorenzini on its snout
Keeps its muscles, eyes and brain warmer than the surrounding water with a heat-exchanging circulation
Launches fully out of the water when ambushing seals from below
Migrates across oceans: one female swam from South Africa to Australia and back, about 20,000 km, in nine months

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, rays and other sharks when young; seals, sea lions, dolphins and whale carcasses as adults
animal.habitat: Coastal and offshore waters, usually 12–24 °C, from the surface to over 1,000 m
animal.size: Usually 3.5–5 m; large females to ~6 m and over 2 t
animal.behaviour: California white sharks gather each winter and spring at a mid-Pacific spot nicknamed the 'White Shark Café', between Baja California and Hawaii.
fieldMarks: Grey above, white below with a sharp border
Black tips to the underside of the pectoral fins
Conical snout and large triangular teeth
animal.lookalikes: Shortfin mako is slimmer and more blue, with long curved teeth. Basking shark has huge gill slits and a tiny mouth. Avoid swimming where whites are present.
animal.whereToSee: Neptune Islands (South Australia, cage diving), Cape Cod (Massachusetts) and the Farallon Islands (California)
animal.season: Cape Cod Jul–Oct; Farallones Sep–Nov; Neptune Islands all year

lore: Peter Benchley's novel Jaws (1974) and Spielberg's 1975 film made the great white a figure of fear; Benchley later spent years campaigning for shark conservation. Some Māori coastal tribes honour sharks as kaitiaki (guardians).
funFact: Orcas off South Africa have been seen killing great whites to eat their livers, and the sharks then abandon the area for months.

summary: The largest living fish, a slow-moving filter feeder that can grow longer than a bus. Despite its size it eats plankton, fish eggs and small fish, and it is harmless to divers.
nativeRange: Tropical and warm-temperate seas worldwide; aggregations at Ningaloo (Australia), Yucatán (Mexico), Donsol and Oslob (Philippines), the Maldives and the Gulf of Oman
abilities: Filters plankton through spongy pads across its gills, swallowing by suction as well as by swimming forward
Dives to nearly 2,000 m
Migrates thousands of kilometres to seasonal feeding sites, such as spawning coral and fish
Each shark's spot pattern is unique and is matched using an algorithm built for mapping stars

animal.diet: Filter feeder: plankton, krill, fish and coral eggs, small fish and squid
animal.habitat: Warm open ocean and plankton-rich coasts
animal.size: Usually 5–12 m; largest reliably measured about 18–19 m; up to ~20 t
animal.behaviour: A female caught off Taiwan in 1995 carried about 300 embryos at different stages, showing that the species hatches eggs inside the mother and gives birth to live young.
fieldMarks: Largest fish; flattened head and wide mouth at the front
Dark grey with pale spots and stripes
animal.lookalikes: Basking shark lacks spots and has huge gill slits.
animal.whereToSee: Ningaloo Reef (Australia), Isla Holbox and Isla Mujeres (Mexico) and Donsol (Philippines)
animal.season: Ningaloo Mar–Jul; Mexico Jun–Sep; Donsol about Dec–May

lore: Japanese fishermen called it Ebisu-zame after the god of fishing and good fortune, because schools of fish gathered around it.
funFact: Its skin can be up to about 10 cm thick, among the thickest of any animal.

otherNames: Shuāngwěn qiánkǒu fúfèn 双吻前口蝠鲼 (Chinese)
summary: The largest ray, with a wingspan of up to about 7 m. It glides through the open ocean filtering plankton and visits reef 'cleaning stations' where small fish pick off parasites.
nativeRange: Tropical, subtropical and temperate oceans worldwide, mostly offshore and around oceanic islands
abilities: Has the largest brain relative to body size of any fish
Captive mantas reacted to their reflection in ways that suggest self-awareness
Funnels plankton into its mouth with cephalic fins that unroll like scoops
Leaps clear of the water and somersaults while feeding
Each individual's belly spot pattern is unique and lifelong

animal.diet: Filter feeder: zooplankton, krill, fish larvae
animal.habitat: Open ocean, upwelling zones, seamounts and offshore reefs
animal.size: Wingspan usually 4.5–7 m; up to ~2 t
animal.behaviour: Females give birth to a single pup every two to five years, one of the slowest reproductive rates of any fish.
fieldMarks: Two cephalic fins in front of the mouth
Black above with white shoulder patches
animal.lookalikes: Reef manta (Mobula alfredi) is smaller with shoulder patches that curve inward. Devil rays are smaller with mouths on the underside.
animal.whereToSee: Revillagigedo Islands (Socorro), Mexico; Isla de la Plata (Ecuador)

lore: Spanish-speaking pearl divers named it manta, 'blanket', and sailors' 'devil-fish' tales told of mantas wrapping and drowning divers, which are untrue. Its gill plates are now traded as a modern health tonic, the main threat to the species.
funFact: Mantas are close relatives of sharks and have no stinging spine, unlike stingrays.

summary: A small, upright-swimming fish of Indo-Pacific estuaries and seagrass beds in which the male, not the female, becomes pregnant. Its species name comes from the Malay word for horse.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from India and the Persian Gulf to Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines and Hawaii
abilities: Males carry fertilised eggs in a brood pouch, supply them with oxygen and give birth to live young
Anchors itself with a prehensile tail
Moves each eye independently
Sucks prey into its tube-like snout in a few milliseconds
Changes colour to match its surroundings

animal.diet: Carnivore: copepods, small shrimp and other tiny crustaceans
animal.habitat: Shallow seagrass, estuaries, mangroves and harbours, often in murky water
animal.size: Up to ~17 cm
animal.behaviour: Paired seahorses often greet each other each morning with a 'dance' of changing colour and linked tails.
fieldMarks: Upright seahorse with a curled tail
Yellow, black or brown with fine spots
animal.lookalikes: Other Indo-Pacific seahorses are very similar; experts check spines, crown and ring counts.

lore: Its form recalls the hippocampus, the sea-horse that pulled Poseidon's chariot in Greek myth, and Conrad Gessner illustrated seahorses in his Historiae animalium (1558). Dried seahorses (hǎimǎ) are a long-standing ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, which drives much of the trade in wild seahorses.
funFact: A male can give birth to hundreds of babies at once.

summary: An orange-and-white reef fish that lives unharmed among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones. All clownfish hatch male, and the largest fish in a group becomes the breeding female.
nativeRange: Eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific: Andaman Sea, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, northern Australia, Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands
abilities: A mucus coat keeps it from triggering the stinging cells of its host anemone
Changes sex from male to female if the group's female dies
Defends its anemone, removes parasites and feeds it with scraps and nitrogen from its waste
Larvae find their way home to reefs by following smell and sound

animal.diet: Omnivore: zooplankton, algae, small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow lagoons and reefs, in host anemones such as Heteractis magnifica and Stichodactyla gigantea
animal.lifespan: 6–10 years in the wild; 20+ in aquariums
animal.size: Up to ~11 cm
animal.behaviour: Each anemone holds a strict size-ranked group: one breeding female, her male partner and several smaller non-breeders that wait their turn.
fieldMarks: Small orange fish with three white bands
Thin black edging around the bands and fins
animal.lookalikes: Orange clownfish (A. percula) has thicker black edges around the white bands and usually 10 dorsal spines, versus 11 in A. ocellaris, which has a taller dorsal fin.
animal.whereToSee: Coral reefs of Bali (Tulamben and Amed) and the Similan Islands (Thailand)

lore: Pixar's Finding Nemo (2003) made this species the world's best-known reef fish and boosted aquarium demand; it was one of the first marine fish bred routinely in captivity.
funFact: Clownfish 'talk' to each other with clicks and pops made by snapping their jaws.

summary: A lobe-finned 'living fossil' known only from fossils and believed extinct for 66 million years until a fisherman's catch in South Africa in 1938. Its fleshy fins and ancient lineage make it a cousin of the fish that first walked onto land.
nativeRange: Western Indian Ocean: Comoros, Mozambique, South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya and Madagascar
abilities: Moves its paired lobed fins in an alternating pattern like the legs of a walking tetrapod
Senses prey's electric fields with a jelly-filled rostral organ in its snout
Drifts head-down in 'headstands' while hunting
Opens its mouth unusually wide thanks to a hinged joint in its skull
Lives about a century and carries its young for around five years

animal.diet: Carnivore: fish, squid and cuttlefish
animal.habitat: Steep volcanic slopes at 150–700 m; shelters in caves by day
animal.size: Up to ~2 m and ~90 kg
animal.behaviour: By day small groups share the same lava caves, then drift out alone at night to hunt along the slope.
fieldMarks: Large, deep blue fish with white blotches
animal.season: Resident; hides in caves by day

lore: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted one in a trawler's catch at East London, South Africa, in December 1938 and the ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith named it for her. Comorian fishermen had long known the fish, which they called gombessa.
funFact: A second species, Latimeria menadoensis, was found in an Indonesian fish market in 1997, about 10,000 km away.

summary: A clever, short-lived mollusc of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic, with three hearts, blue blood and most of its neurons in its arms. It changes colour and skin texture in an instant to vanish against rock or sand.
nativeRange: Mediterranean Sea and eastern Atlantic; similar species elsewhere were long included under this name
abilities: Changes colour, pattern and skin texture within a fraction of a second using chromatophores and papillae
Arms, holding about two-thirds of its neurons, can taste, touch and act semi-independently
Solves puzzles, unscrews jars and learns by watching another octopus
Squeezes through any gap larger than its hard beak
Squirts ink clouds and jets away by water propulsion

animal.diet: Carnivore: crabs, clams, snails, fish
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts, reefs and seagrass from shallows to ~200 m
animal.size: Mantle up to ~25 cm; arm span to ~1 m; usually 3–10 kg
animal.behaviour: A female guards and cleans her eggs in a den for weeks without eating, and dies soon after they hatch.
fieldMarks: Lives in dens with shell piles outside
animal.lookalikes: Several similar octopuses elsewhere were long called 'common octopus'.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky shores of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic

lore: Octopuses sprawl across Minoan 'Marine Style' jars from Crete (c. 1500 BCE), and Aristotle's History of Animals describes their mating and colour change. Pliny tells of an octopus at Carteia in Spain that raided a fish-salting works by night.
funFact: Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.

summary: A deep-sea squid that can reach about 12–13 m including its long feeding tentacles, almost certainly the source of the kraken legend. It was not photographed alive in its own habitat until 2004.
nativeRange: Deep waters of all oceans; most records from Newfoundland, Norway, New Zealand, South Africa, Japan and the Bay of Biscay
abilities: Has eyes up to ~27 cm across, the largest in the animal kingdom alongside the colossal squid's
Grips prey with hundreds of suckers lined with toothed rings
Stays buoyant using ammonium-rich tissues lighter than seawater
Survives as a staple prey of sperm whales, which bear sucker scars from fighting them

animal.diet: Carnivore: deep-sea fish and other squid
animal.habitat: Mid-depths, roughly 300–1,000 m
animal.size: Females up to ~12–13 m total length, ~275 kg; males smaller
animal.behaviour: Its vast eyes are thought to help it spot the glow that sperm whales stir up in bioluminescent plankton from over 100 m away.
fieldMarks: Huge squid with eight arms and two very long feeding tentacles
Eyes as large as dinner plates
animal.lookalikes: Colossal squid (Antarctic) is heavier with hooks on its suckers.

lore: Bishop Erik Pontoppidan's Natural History of Norway (1752–53) described the kraken, a sea monster big enough to be mistaken for an island. Japetus Steenstrup named the genus in 1857 from a beak washed ashore in Denmark, and Jules Verne used it in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas.
funFact: Its doughnut-shaped brain surrounds the oesophagus, so swallowing large food could damage it; it cuts food into small pieces with its beak.

otherNames: Quèwěi tángláng xiā 雀尾螳螂虾 (Chinese)
summary: A rainbow-coloured crustacean of Indo-Pacific reefs with one of the fastest punches in the animal kingdom. Its spring-loaded clubs smash snail shells and crab armour, and its eyes see colours and light polarisation in ways no other animal is known to.
nativeRange: Indo-Pacific from East Africa to Guam, the Philippines and northern Australia
abilities: Strikes with its club at about 23 m/s, with an acceleration comparable to a .22-calibre bullet
Each strike forms collapsing cavitation bubbles that deliver a second shock to prey
Has 12–16 types of photoreceptor and sees ultraviolet and circularly polarised light
Each eye judges depth on its own, using three separate zones
Its club's spiral (helicoidal) structure absorbs impacts and has inspired new composite materials

animal.diet: Carnivore: snails, crabs, clams, worms
animal.habitat: U-shaped burrows in rubble and sand near coral reefs, 3–40 m
animal.behaviour: It lines the entrance of its burrow with rubble and is known to strike at divers' fingers, which is why aquarists call it a 'thumb-splitter'.
fieldMarks: Brightly coloured green, red and blue
Club-like raptorial limbs folded under the head
animal.lookalikes: Other mantis shrimps. Its strike can break aquarium glass and cut fingers; do not handle.
animal.whereToSee: Lembeh Strait (Indonesia) and Anilao (Philippines)

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1758 as Cancer scyllarus. Hobbyists tell stories of mantis shrimps cracking aquarium glass, and their punch has been studied with high-speed cameras since the 2000s.
funFact: A mantis shrimp's club regrows each time the animal moults.

summary: A plump, eight-legged micro-animal about a quarter of a millimetre long and the main laboratory model for studying tardigrades. Like many tardigrades it can survive drying out and freezing by shutting its body down almost entirely.
nativeRange: Described in 2018 from a long-running laboratory culture originating in the UK; tardigrades as a group occur worldwide
abilities: Survives slow drying by curling into a 'tun' and entering cryptobiosis, with metabolism nearly stopped
Tolerates freezing and recovers when thawed
Protects its cells while drying with tardigrade-specific disordered proteins that form a glassy state
Reproduces without males (parthenogenesis), so one animal can found a whole culture

animal.diet: Algae such as Chlorococcum, sucked from cells through a stylet-armed mouth
animal.habitat: Freshwater sediment and aquatic plants
animal.lifespan: A few weeks to a few months when active
animal.behaviour: It lumbers on eight stubby clawed legs and moults its cuticle as it grows, often laying eggs in the shed skin.
fieldMarks: Barrel-shaped body with eight stubby legs
animal.lookalikes: Other tardigrades need microscopy to identify.

lore: The pastor Johann Goeze named tardigrades 'kleiner Wasserbär' (little water bear) in 1773, and Lazzaro Spallanzani gave them the name tardigrado, 'slow stepper', in 1776 after reviving them from dust. This species was long misidentified as Hypsibius dujardini until it was described in 2018.
funFact: Its genome, sequenced in the 2010s, sparked debate over claims that tardigrades had borrowed large amounts of foreign DNA; later analyses found that most of it was contamination.

otherNames: Dēngtǎ shuǐmǔ 灯塔水母, 'lighthouse jellyfish' (Chinese)
summary: A tiny hydrozoan jellyfish, a few millimetres across, that can reverse its own life cycle. When injured, starving or aged, the adult medusa can turn back into a polyp and start again, so in principle it never has to die of old age.
nativeRange: Described from the Mediterranean; similar Turritopsis are found in temperate and tropical seas worldwide
abilities: Reverts from adult medusa to an early polyp stage through transdifferentiation, turning specialised cells into other cell types
Can repeat this rejuvenation many times
Buds many genetically identical medusae from a single polyp colony
Catches plankton with stinging tentacles

animal.diet: Zooplankton, fish eggs, small larvae
animal.habitat: Coastal plankton; polyps attached to hard surfaces
animal.lifespan: Potentially unlimited, though most are eaten or die of disease
animal.size: Medusa ~4–5 mm across
animal.behaviour: The bell is transparent with a bright red gut and up to about 90 tentacles.
fieldMarks: Many fine tentacles around the bell rim
animal.lookalikes: Other Turritopsis species are almost identical; genetics is often needed.

lore: German student Christian Sommer noticed the life-cycle reversal while keeping specimens collected off Rapallo, Italy, in 1988; Ferdinando Boero and Stefano Piraino's team described it in 1996.
funFact: A few other jellyfish, including a moon jelly, have since been found to rejuvenate in a similar way, but Turritopsis dohrnii remains the best-studied case.

summary: A fast-growing, antler-branched reef-building coral that once formed dense thickets across Caribbean reefs. Since the 1980s disease and bleaching have killed most of it, and it is now a focus of coral nursery restoration.
nativeRange: Caribbean Sea, the Bahamas, Florida Keys and southern Gulf of Mexico
abilities: Grows 10–20 cm a year in branch length, among the fastest of Atlantic corals
Lays down a limestone skeleton that builds reef framework
Hosts photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) in its tissues, which supply most of its energy
Regrows into new colonies from broken branches, the basis of coral 'gardening'
Releases egg-sperm bundles in mass spawning nights after the summer full moon

animal.diet: Mainly sugars from symbiotic algae; also captures plankton with tiny polyp tentacles
animal.habitat: Shallow, clear fore-reef and back-reef zones, typically 5–20 m
animal.lifespan: Colonies can persist indefinitely by fragmenting
animal.size: Branches 1–3 cm thick; thickets can cover large areas
animal.behaviour: Its thickets shelter juvenile fish, lobsters and other reef life.
animal.lookalikes: Elkhorn coral (A. palmata) has broad, flattened branches. Fused staghorn (A. prolifera) is a hybrid with thicker, fused branches.
animal.whereToSee: Coral Restoration Foundation sites in the Florida Keys and Bonaire

lore: In 2006 staghorn and elkhorn corals became the first corals listed under the US Endangered Species Act. Restoration groups in Florida and the Caribbean have since grown and planted tens of thousands of nursery fragments.
funFact: White-band disease in the 1980s killed an estimated 80–98% of Caribbean staghorn and elkhorn coral.

summary: Not a crab at all but a relative of spiders and scorpions, from a lineage whose body plan has changed little for over 400 million years. Its blue blood is used to test vaccines and medical equipment for bacterial contamination.
nativeRange: Atlantic coast of North America from Maine to the Gulf of Mexico and Yucatán; largest spawning in Delaware Bay
abilities: Blood cells (amoebocytes) clot instantly around bacterial endotoxins, the basis of the LAL test
Has ten eyes, including large compound eyes that become a million times more sensitive to light at night
Rights itself with its long tail (telson) when flipped over
Mass spawning on spring high tides gives migrating shorebirds such as red knots a key food source

animal.diet: Clams, worms, small crustaceans and other bottom invertebrates
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters and estuaries; spawns on sandy beaches
animal.size: Females up to ~60 cm long including tail; males smaller
animal.behaviour: On spring nights near new and full moons, females crawl ashore at high tide to lay thousands of eggs, with males clinging behind.
animal.whereToSee: Delaware Bay beaches, e.g. Reeds Beach (New Jersey) and Slaughter Beach (Delaware)
animal.season: Spawning May–Jun, on high tides near new and full moons

uses.use: Limulus amebocyte lysate (LAL) from the blood detects bacterial endotoxins in vaccines, injectable drugs and implants

medicinal.cautions: Bled crabs are returned to the sea, but an estimated 10–30% die. Synthetic recombinant Factor C tests are an approved alternative.

lore: Coastal Indigenous peoples used the shells to bail canoes and the tails as spear tips, and colonial farmers ground millions of horseshoe crabs into fertiliser. Frederik Bang's discovery in the 1950s that its blood clots on contact with bacteria led to the LAL test.
funFact: Studies of its large optic nerves helped H. Keffer Hartline win the 1967 Nobel Prize for discoveries about how eyes process images.

summary: A silver ocean-going fish that is born in cold rivers, feeds in the North Atlantic and returns by smell to spawn in the stream where it hatched. Wild numbers have fallen sharply, even as farmed Atlantic salmon fill supermarkets worldwide.
nativeRange: Rivers and seas of the North Atlantic, from Portugal to the Barents Sea, Iceland, Greenland and north-eastern North America
abilities: Navigates thousands of kilometres back to its home river using the magnetic field and smell
Leaps waterfalls and weirs over 3 m high
Switches its body chemistry between fresh and salt water during smoltification
Unlike Pacific salmon, some survive spawning and return to spawn again
Carries marine nutrients upstream, feeding river and riverside ecosystems when it dies

animal.diet: Young eat aquatic insects; adults at sea eat fish such as capelin, herring and sand eels, and krill
animal.habitat: Clean, cold gravel-bedded rivers for breeding; North Atlantic feeding grounds
animal.size: Usually 60–110 cm and 2–10 kg; record ~1.5 m and ~46 kg
animal.behaviour: Young salmon (parr) stay in fresh water for one to eight years, then turn silver and head out to sea as smolts.
fieldMarks: Streamlined silver fish with small black spots
Slim tail base and forked tail
Upper jaw ends below the eye
Spawning males turn bronze-red with a hooked jaw
animal.lookalikes: Sea trout (brown trout) has a thicker tail base, a squarer tail and an upper jaw reaching past the eye.
animal.whereToSee: Falls of Shin (Scotland) and the River Spey
animal.season: Rivers year-round; leaping at Falls of Shin Jun–Sep; spawning Nov–Dec

lore: In Irish legend the young Fionn mac Cumhaill burned his thumb cooking the Salmon of Knowledge (Bradán Feasa) and gained all the world's wisdom. A salmon carved about 25,000 years ago in the rock shelter of Abri du Poisson, France, is one of the oldest fish images known.
funFact: IUCN moved the Atlantic salmon to Near Threatened in 2023 after its global population fell by about 23% between 2006 and 2020.

summary: A snake-like fish that lives for decades in European rivers and lakes, then swims some 5,000 km to spawn in the Sargasso Sea and die. No one has yet seen European eels spawn in the wild.
nativeRange: Rivers, lakes and coasts of Europe and North Africa, from Iceland and Norway to the Mediterranean and Morocco; spawns in the Sargasso Sea
abilities: Migrates about 5,000–6,000 km across the Atlantic to spawn
Changes form several times: leaf-like larva, transparent glass eel, elver, yellow eel and silver eel
Breathes partly through its skin and can wriggle across wet grass between waters
Adjusts its eyes and body chemistry for the deep ocean before its final migration

animal.diet: Carnivore and scavenger: insect larvae, worms, crustaceans, fish, carrion
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes, ponds, estuaries and coastal lagoons
animal.lifespan: Usually 5–20 years in fresh water; can exceed 80 in captivity
animal.size: Females up to ~1.3 m; males usually under 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Larvae drift on the Gulf Stream for about one to three years before arriving at European coasts as see-through glass eels.
fieldMarks: Dorsal fin starts well behind the pectoral fins
Lower jaw slightly longer than the upper
animal.lookalikes: Conger eel is marine, with the dorsal fin starting just behind the pectoral fins and an upper jaw that projects. Lampreys have no jaws.
animal.whereToSee: Elver runs on the River Severn (England)
animal.season: Glass eels arrive Feb–May; silver eels leave in autumn on dark nights
