lore: Aristotle concluded that eels arose spontaneously from mud, and a young Sigmund Freud dissected hundreds in Trieste in 1876 hunting for their testes. The Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt traced ever-smaller larvae to the Sargasso Sea between 1904 and 1922.
funFact: Glass eels arriving in Europe have fallen by over 90% since the 1980s, and illegal trafficking of them to Asia has been called one of the largest wildlife crimes in Europe.

summary: A large European earthworm that digs deep vertical burrows and drags fallen leaves underground at night. Its burrowing mixes and aerates soil, and Charles Darwin spent decades measuring how much earth worms move.
nativeRange: Europe; introduced to North America, New Zealand and elsewhere, where it is invasive in some previously worm-free northern forests
abilities: Digs permanent vertical burrows up to ~2 m deep that let air and water into the soil
Pulls leaves into its burrow, mixing organic matter deep into the soil
Breathes entirely through its moist skin
Senses light with cells in its skin despite having no eyes
As a hermaphrodite, each worm both gives and receives sperm when mating

animal.diet: Detritivore: dead leaves, decaying plant matter and soil microbes
animal.habitat: Moist, loamy soils of meadows, woods, fields and gardens
animal.lifespan: Several years; up to ~6 in captivity
animal.size: Usually 15–25 cm; up to ~35 cm
animal.behaviour: On damp nights it stretches out of its burrow to feed and mate, keeping its tail anchored inside so it can snap back at the slightest vibration.
fieldMarks: Reddish-brown front end fading toward the rear
animal.lookalikes: Aporrectodea trapezoides is similar in size and dark colour.
animal.whereToSee: Lawns and fields after rain
animal.season: Active all year in moist soil

lore: Darwin's last book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms (1881), showed how earthworms slowly bury stones and ancient ruins. It was a bestseller in its day.
funFact: In northern North American forests that lost their native worms in the last Ice Age, this introduced species eats away the leaf litter that native wildflowers and salamanders depend on.

summary: A stocky, fearless mustelid of Africa and southern Asia, famed for raiding beehives and fighting off lions. Thick, loose skin lets it twist round and bite an attacker that has hold of it.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa's edges, Arabia, Iran, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent
abilities: Resists cobra and other snake venom because of a mutation in its nerve receptors, shared with mongooses
Rips open beehives, termite mounds and burrows with long, strong foreclaws
Escapes and solves problems: captive honey badgers have stacked objects to climb out of enclosures
Releases a foul smell from anal glands when threatened

animal.diet: Omnivore: rodents, snakes, lizards, insects, bee larvae and honey, carrion, fruit
animal.habitat: Almost every habitat from desert to forest edge
animal.lifespan: 7–8 years in the wild; to ~24 in captivity
animal.size: Males 9–16 kg, females 5–10 kg; body 55–77 cm
animal.behaviour: Mainly a solitary forager, it may travel 10–30 km in a day of digging for prey. Its partnership with honeyguide birds is widely told but poorly documented.
fieldMarks: Black below with a silver-grey back
Short legs with long front claws
animal.voice: Growls and rattles
animal.lookalikes: Zorilla (striped polecat) is smaller with black-and-white stripes. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (South Africa/Botswana)

lore: Afrikaans-speaking farmers called it the ratel, a name that entered zoology. The 2011 viral video 'The Crazy Nastyass Honey Badger' made its fearlessness an internet legend.
funFact: Bitten by a cobra, a honey badger may collapse, sleep for a couple of hours, then wake up and finish eating the snake.

summary: The one-humped camel, domesticated in Arabia around 3,000 years ago, made long-distance trade across the Sahara and Arabian deserts possible. It can lose a quarter or more of its body water and recover by drinking over 100 litres in minutes.
nativeRange: Domesticated in Arabia; no wild populations survive. Kept across North Africa, the Horn of Africa, Arabia, West and South Asia; large feral population in Australia
abilities: Lets its body temperature swing by about 6 °C over a day to avoid sweating away water
Loses up to about 25–30% of its body weight in water and survives
Has oval red blood cells that keep flowing when it is dehydrated and can swell without bursting when it drinks fast
Closes its nostrils and shields its eyes with long double lashes during sandstorms
Stores fat, not water, in its hump, which it uses for energy when food is scarce

animal.diet: Herbivore: thorny shrubs, saltbush, dry grasses; can eat salty plants other livestock avoid
animal.habitat: Hot deserts and dry scrub
animal.size: 1.8–2 m at the shoulder; 300–600 kg
animal.behaviour: Camels walk by moving both legs on the same side together (pacing), which gives a rolling stride. Their broad, padded feet spread out on soft sand.
animal.voice: Loud groans and roars
animal.lookalikes: Bactrian camel has two humps.
animal.whereToSee: Desert markets and camps of Arabia and North Africa

lore: The Qur'an (88:17) asks 'Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?', and the she-camel of the prophet Salih is a sign of God. Nabataean caravans of dromedaries carried incense from Arabia to Petra and the Mediterranean.
funFact: Camel milk does not curdle easily, so it is hard to make into cheese; a special enzyme was developed to make camel cheese possible.

summary: North America's heaviest land animal, which once roamed the Great Plains in herds of tens of millions. Hunted down to fewer than a thousand by the late 1880s, it has recovered to about half a million, though few are wild herds.
nativeRange: Great Plains and western North America from Alaska and Canada to northern Mexico; now mostly in parks, reserves and ranches
abilities: Runs at up to ~55 km/h despite weighing up to a tonne
Swings its massive head to clear deep snow and reach grass
Rolls in dust wallows that become seasonal pools and microhabitats
Grazing patterns create a patchwork of short and tall grass that benefits prairie dogs, birds and plants

animal.diet: Herbivore: mainly grasses and sedges
animal.habitat: Open grassland, prairie and meadow; wood bison in boreal clearings
animal.size: Bulls up to ~1.9 m at the shoulder and ~900–1,000 kg; cows ~450 kg
animal.behaviour: Bulls bellow and butt heads during the summer rut. Herds once followed seasonal grazing across hundreds of kilometres.
fieldMarks: Shaggy brown front and short back hair
Short curved horns in both sexes
animal.voice: Bulls bellow during the rut
animal.lookalikes: Domestic cattle lack the hump. Stay at least 25 yards away (US park rule).
animal.whereToSee: Lamar and Hayden valleys (Yellowstone); Custer State Park and Wind Cave National Park (South Dakota)

lore: Lakota tradition tells how White Buffalo Calf Woman brought the sacred pipe, and the birth of a white calf is still seen as a sacred sign. Coronado's 1541 expedition described the 'vacas de Cíbola' covering the plains.
funFact: In 2016 the bison became the national mammal of the United States.

summary: The largest land carnivore, a bear that lives on Arctic sea ice and hunts seals. It is classed as a marine mammal, and the loss of summer sea ice is its greatest threat.
nativeRange: Circumpolar Arctic: Canada, Alaska (USA), Greenland, Norway (Svalbard) and Russia
abilities: Smells seals through snow and ice from about a kilometre away
Swims for days; one female swam 687 km over nine days without rest
Survives Arctic cold with up to 11 cm of fat, black skin and hollow, colourless guard hairs
Fasts for months during ice-free summers, slowing its metabolism

animal.diet: Carnivore: mainly ringed and bearded seals; also walrus, whale carcasses, birds' eggs
animal.habitat: Sea ice over continental shelves; coasts in summer
animal.size: Males 350–700 kg and up to ~2.5–3 m; females 150–300 kg
animal.behaviour: Pregnant females dig snow dens and give birth in midwinter, nursing cubs for months without eating before leading them out to the ice in spring.
animal.lookalikes: Brown bears have a shoulder hump and brown fur. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Churchill (Manitoba) by tundra vehicle; Svalbard by boat

lore: Inuit hunters treat nanuq with great respect in story and ritual; one Inuit name, Pihoqahiak, means 'the ever-wandering one'. In 1252 King Henry III kept a polar bear, a gift from Norway, at the Tower of London, where it fished in the Thames on a long chain.
funFact: Eating polar bear liver can kill a person, because it holds a toxic concentration of vitamin A.

summary: The northernmost non-human primate, a red-faced monkey that survives snowy winters in the mountains of Japan. Some troops have learned habits, like bathing in hot springs, that spread from monkey to monkey, an early example of animal culture.
nativeRange: Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and nearby small islands, Japan
abilities: Survives winters at −15 °C with thick fur and by huddling
Troops at Jigokudani soak in volcanic hot springs in winter, which lowers their stress hormones
On Kōshima, a young female named Imo started washing sweet potatoes in the sea in 1953, and the habit spread through the troop
Some troops roll snowballs for play

animal.diet: Omnivore: fruit, seeds, leaves, bark, insects; bark and buds in winter
animal.habitat: Subtropical to subalpine forests
animal.size: Males ~10–14 kg; females ~8–10 kg; short tail
animal.behaviour: Troops are organised around ranked lines of related females. Males leave their birth troop and join others.
animal.voice: Coos and barks
animal.lookalikes: The only monkey in Japan.
animal.whereToSee: Jigokudani Monkey Park (Nagano)

lore: The 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil' monkeys carved at the Tōshō-gū shrine in Nikkō (17th century) are Japanese macaques. Monkeys are messengers of the Sannō deity at Hiyoshi Taisha shrine.
funFact: The hot-spring bathing began in 1963, when a young female at Jigokudani followed soybeans into a pool and others copied her.

summary: An Arctic whale whose males grow a spiralled tusk up to about 3 m long, which is actually a tooth that grows through the upper lip. Medieval Europeans sold these tusks as unicorn horns.
nativeRange: Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland, Svalbard and Russia, mainly the Atlantic Arctic and Baffin Bay
abilities: Grows a tusk, usually the left canine, that spirals counter-clockwise and can reach ~3 m
The tusk has nerve-linked channels that may sense changes in the surrounding water
Dives to about 1,500 m or more, repeatedly, to hunt halibut in winter
Hunts and navigates under dense pack ice by echolocation
Has been filmed tapping Arctic cod with its tusk to stun them

animal.diet: Greenland halibut, Arctic and polar cod, squid, shrimp
animal.habitat: Deep fjords and offshore pack ice
animal.size: Body 4–5.5 m (not counting tusk); 800–1,600 kg
animal.behaviour: Narwhals migrate seasonally between summer fjords and winter feeding grounds under dense pack ice. Males sometimes rub tusks together ('tusking').
fieldMarks: Males have a long, spiral tusk
animal.voice: Clicks, whistles and knocks
animal.lookalikes: Beluga is white with no tusk.
animal.whereToSee: Floe edge near Pond Inlet and Arctic Bay (Nunavut)

lore: The Danish kings' coronation throne at Rosenborg Castle (1660s) is made largely of narwhal tusk, then believed to be unicorn horn. An Inuit story tells of a cruel woman dragged into the sea by a harpooned narwhal, her twisted hair becoming its tusk.
funFact: About 1 in 500 males grows two tusks, and a few females grow one.

summary: The only living relative of the giraffe, a shy forest animal with a reddish body and zebra-striped legs, found only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was unknown to Western science until 1901.
nativeRange: Rainforests of northern, central and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially the Ituri Forest
abilities: Strips leaves with a long, dark, prehensile tongue it can also use to clean its eyes and ears
Calls to its calf with infrasound below human hearing
Striped hindquarters break up its outline in the dappled forest light
Eats over a hundred species of plants, including some that are poisonous to people

animal.diet: Herbivore: leaves, buds, shoots, ferns, fruit and fungi; eats clay and charcoal for minerals
animal.habitat: Dense tropical rainforest at 500–1,500 m
animal.size: 1.5 m at shoulder; 200–350 kg
animal.behaviour: Newborn calves hide in a nest for weeks and do not defecate for the first month or two, which may help keep predators from finding them.
animal.lookalikes: Its striped legs suggest a zebra, but zebras are striped all over; its only close relative, the giraffe, lives in open savanna.
animal.whereToSee: Okapi Wildlife Reserve (Epulu)

lore: Henry Morton Stanley heard of a forest 'donkey' in the 1890s, and in 1901 Harry Johnston sent skin to London, where it was named for him. The okapi is a national symbol of the DRC and appears on its banknotes.
funFact: It was first named as a horse species, Equus johnstoni, before skulls showed it was a giraffid.

summary: A nocturnal lemur of Madagascar with bat-like ears, rodent-like teeth and a strange, skeletal middle finger. It finds grubs by tapping on wood and listening for hollow tunnels.
nativeRange: Madagascar, mainly the eastern rainforests and scattered western and northern forests
abilities: Taps wood with its thin middle finger and listens to find hollow insect tunnels (percussive foraging)
Gnaws into wood with ever-growing incisors, then hooks out larvae with that ball-jointed finger
Has an extra 'pseudothumb' on each wrist
Turns its large ears independently to locate sounds

animal.diet: Omnivore: wood-boring beetle larvae, seeds, nectar, fungi, coconuts and other fruit
animal.habitat: Rainforest, dry forest, mangroves and plantations
animal.lifespan: Poorly known in the wild; 20+ years in captivity
animal.size: 2–2.6 kg; body ~40 cm with a bushy tail of 45–55 cm
animal.behaviour: The world's largest nocturnal primate, it spends the day curled in a ball-shaped nest of leaves high in the canopy.
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Nosy Mangabe Special Reserve

lore: In parts of Madagascar, local fady (taboos) hold the aye-aye to be a sign of death and it may be killed on sight. Pierre Sonnerat brought the first description to Europe in 1782, and early naturalists classed it as a squirrel.
funFact: It is the only primate known to find food by tapping and listening, a method otherwise used by woodpeckers.

summary: The smallest wild canid, a cream-coloured desert fox whose ears can be 15 cm long. Those huge ears give off body heat and pick up prey moving under the sand.
nativeRange: Sahara and adjoining deserts of North Africa, from Morocco and Mauritania to Egypt and Sudan; Sinai
abilities: Hears insects and rodents moving underground with its enormous ears
Sheds heat through ears full of blood vessels
Can go long periods without drinking, getting water from its food
Walks on hot sand with thickly furred soles
Can dig up to about 6 m of burrow in a single night

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects, rodents, lizards, birds' eggs, roots and fruit
animal.habitat: Sandy desert and dune fields
animal.lifespan: ~10 years in the wild; up to 14+ in captivity
animal.size: 1–1.5 kg; body 24–40 cm, ears to 15 cm
animal.behaviour: Fennecs are nocturnal and live in family groups in sprawling burrows. Pairs often stay together for life.
animal.lookalikes: Rüppell's fox is larger and greyer with smaller ears.
animal.whereToSee: Erg Chebbi (Morocco) and Douz (Tunisia)

lore: The name comes from Arabic fanak, 'fox'. Algeria's national football team is nicknamed Les Fennecs, and the fox in Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (1943) is thought to have been inspired by fennecs he saw in the Sahara.
funFact: Relative to its body, the fennec has the largest ears of any canid.

summary: The fastest land animal, a slender cat built for sprinting down gazelles on open plains. It trades the power of other big cats for speed, and often loses its kills to lions and hyenas.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, scattered Saharan and Sahelian populations; a tiny remnant in Iran; reintroduced to India in 2022
abilities: Sprints at about 93–104 km/h in short bursts
Accelerates from a standstill to about 95 km/h in roughly three seconds
Grips the ground with semi-retractable claws like running spikes
Uses its long tail as a rudder to turn sharply mid-chase
Chirps like a bird and purrs, but cannot roar

animal.diet: Carnivore: gazelles, impala, springbok, hares and young antelope
animal.habitat: Open savanna, grassland and semi-desert
animal.size: 21–72 kg; body 1.1–1.5 m plus a tail of 60–80 cm
animal.behaviour: Females live alone with their cubs, while brothers often stay together for life in male coalitions that hold territories.
fieldMarks: Black tear lines from eyes to mouth
animal.voice: Chirps and purrs
animal.lookalikes: Leopard has rosettes, a heavier build and no tear lines. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Maasai Mara (Kenya), Serengeti (Ndutu) and Kgalagadi

lore: Cheetahs were tamed for hunting from ancient Egypt to medieval Persia and India; the Mughal emperor Akbar was said to keep around a thousand. The black 'tear marks' feature in an African folk tale of a mother weeping for her stolen cubs.
funFact: Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity, probably from a population crash around 10,000 years ago.

summary: A huge, semi-aquatic grazer that spends its days in rivers and lakes and comes ashore at night to graze. Despite its plant diet it is one of Africa's most dangerous animals to people.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, in rivers, lakes and swamps from Senegal and Sudan to South Africa; feral population in Colombia
abilities: Secretes a red 'blood sweat' (hipposudoric acid) that acts as sunscreen and inhibits bacteria
Holds its breath for about five minutes, walking or bouncing along river bottoms instead of swimming
Moves huge amounts of grass-derived nutrients into rivers in its dung, fuelling fish and other life
Opens its mouth to about 150° to show tusks up to ~50 cm long

animal.diet: Herbivore: grazes up to ~40 kg of grass a night
animal.habitat: Rivers, lakes and swamps beside grassland
animal.size: Males usually 1,500–3,200 kg; up to ~1.6 m at the shoulder
animal.behaviour: Males mark territories by spinning their tails to spray dung. Groups of dozens crowd together in the water by day.
fieldMarks: Large head with eyes and nostrils on top
animal.voice: Loud wheezing honks and grunts
animal.lookalikes: Pygmy hippo is smaller and lives in West African forests. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Chobe River (Botswana), South Luangwa (Zambia) and Murchison Falls (Uganda)

lore: In ancient Egypt the hippo goddess Taweret protected women in childbirth, and blue faience hippos were placed in tombs. Many scholars think the Behemoth of the Book of Job was inspired by the hippopotamus.
funFact: Pablo Escobar's four hippos in Colombia have grown into a wild herd of over 150, now the largest hippo population outside Africa.

summary: The tallest living animal, browsing acacia leaves up to nearly 6 m above the ground. Its heart and blood vessels are specially adapted to pump blood all the way up that long neck.
nativeRange: Savannas and woodlands of Sub-Saharan Africa, from Niger and Chad to South Africa
abilities: Reaches leaves up to ~5.5–6 m high
Has a heart of over 10 kg that drives blood pressure about twice a human's
Tight skin on its legs works like a compression stocking to stop blood pooling
Strips thorny acacia with a dark, prehensile tongue about 45 cm long
Can kill a lion with a kick

animal.diet: Herbivore: leaves, shoots and flowers, especially of acacia; up to ~30 kg a day
animal.habitat: Savanna and open woodland
animal.size: Males up to ~5.5 m tall and ~1,200 kg; females smaller
animal.behaviour: Males fight by 'necking', swinging their necks to hit each other with their ossicones. Giraffes sleep only briefly, often standing up.
animal.lookalikes: Patterns vary between giraffe species and subspecies.
animal.whereToSee: Etosha (Namibia), Maasai Mara (Kenya) and Kruger (South Africa)

lore: A giraffe from Malindi reached the Ming court in 1414 with Zheng He's fleets and was hailed as a qilin, an auspicious beast. Lorenzo de' Medici's giraffe caused a sensation in Florence in 1486, as did 'Zarafa', sent by Egypt's ruler to Charles X of France in 1827.
funFact: Despite its length, a giraffe's neck has only seven vertebrae, the same number as a human's.

summary: The largest rhinoceros and, after elephants, the heaviest land animal, a grazer with a wide square lip for cropping grass. Southern white rhinos recovered from perhaps fewer than a hundred around 1900 to over 15,000, though poaching for horn remains a constant threat.
nativeRange: Southern Africa (mainly South Africa, plus Namibia, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Botswana and others); the northern form once ranged from Uganda to Chad
abilities: Mows grass with a broad, square lip, creating short 'grazing lawns' used by other grazers
Communicates through shared dung middens, which carry information about sex, age and breeding state
Has a front horn of compacted keratin that can exceed 1 m
Charges at up to ~40 km/h

animal.diet: Herbivore: short grasses
animal.habitat: Open grassland and savanna with water and shade
animal.size: Males up to ~2,300–3,600 kg and ~1.8 m at the shoulder; females ~1,700 kg
animal.behaviour: Calves walk ahead of their mothers, unlike black rhino calves, which follow behind.
animal.lookalikes: Black rhino has a hooked lip, no neck hump and browses; white rhino calves run ahead of their mother, black rhino calves behind. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Hluhluwe–iMfolozi Park and Kruger (South Africa)

lore: Reserves in Zululand, including Hluhluwe-iMfolozi (1895), sheltered the last southern white rhinos, and 'Operation Rhino' in the 1960s moved them to parks across Africa. The name 'white' is often traced, without firm evidence, to Dutch or Afrikaans wijd, 'wide', for its mouth.
funFact: Only two northern white rhinos, both female, survive; scientists are trying to save the subspecies with IVF and surrogate southern white mothers.

summary: A small, spiny insect-eater of western European gardens, hedgerows and woodland edges. It rolls into a prickly ball when threatened and hibernates through winter.
nativeRange: Western and northern Europe from Iberia and Italy to Scandinavia and western Russia; introduced to New Zealand
abilities: Rolls into a tight ball covered with 5,000–7,000 spines using a ring of muscle under its skin
Hibernates by dropping its body temperature to a few degrees above freezing
'Self-anoints' by frothing at the mouth and spreading saliva over its spines
Partly resists adder venom
Carries a skin fungus that makes natural antibiotics; a 2022 study found this drove MRSA-type resistance in its bacteria long before human antibiotic use

animal.diet: Insectivore: beetles, caterpillars, earthworms, slugs; eggs and carrion
animal.habitat: Woodland edges, hedgerows, parks and suburban gardens
animal.behaviour: Mostly nocturnal, it may roam 1–2 km a night; snuffling and grunting while foraging gave it its name.
animal.voice: Snuffles and snorts
animal.lookalikes: Northern white-breasted hedgehog (E. roumanicus) of eastern Europe has a white chest patch.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens, parks and hedgerows at night

lore: Pliny the Elder claimed hedgehogs gather fruit by rolling on it and carrying it off on their spines, a scene copied in medieval bestiaries. Its old English name 'urchin' gave sea urchins their name.
funFact: IUCN moved it from Least Concern to Near Threatened in 2024 after studies showed declines in many European countries.

summary: A long-legged, blotch-coated hunting dog of African savannas and one of the most successful pack hunters among large carnivores. Packs care for pups and injured members, feeding them by regurgitating meat.
nativeRange: Fragmented populations in eastern and southern Africa (Botswana, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Zambia, Kenya, South Africa, Mozambique) and a few in West Africa
abilities: Runs prey down over several kilometres, at up to ~60 km/h; often succeeds in most chases it starts
Packs 'vote' to start a hunt by sneezing; the more sneezes, the likelier they set off
Shares kills with pups and sick or injured pack members
Its coat pattern of black, yellow and white is unique to each dog

animal.diet: Carnivore: impala, kudu, gazelles, wildebeest calves
animal.habitat: Savanna, open woodland and semi-desert, with very large home ranges
animal.size: 18–36 kg; ~75 cm at shoulder
animal.behaviour: Usually only the dominant pair breeds, and the whole pack helps raise the litter of up to 10–20 pups.
fieldMarks: Blotched coat of black, brown, yellow and white
animal.voice: Twittering, hoo calls and sneezes
animal.lookalikes: Spotted hyena has a sloping back, spots and round ears. Never approach on foot; watch from a vehicle, boat or hide, or with a licensed guide.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger (South Africa), Moremi (Okavango Delta) and Mana Pools (Zimbabwe)

lore: Coenraad Temminck described it in 1820 as Hyaena picta, 'painted hyena'; its genus name Lycaon, after the king turned into a wolf in Greek myth, came later. Conservationists have popularised the name 'painted wolf' to counter its old reputation as vermin.
funFact: Unlike other dogs, it has only four toes on each front foot.

otherNames: Fēilǜbīn yǎnjìnghóu 菲律宾眼镜猴 (Chinese)
summary: A palm-sized nocturnal primate of the southern Philippines, with each eye about as large as its brain. It is entirely carnivorous, leaping onto insects in the dark.
nativeRange: Southern and eastern Philippines: Bohol, Samar, Leyte, Mindanao and nearby islands
abilities: Turns its head nearly 180° in each direction, since its huge eyes cannot move in their sockets
Communicates with calls of up to about 70 kHz, in pure ultrasound that predators and people cannot hear
Leaps several metres between trunks with long hind legs and elongated ankle bones
Catches insects in mid-air with its hands

animal.diet: Carnivore: insects, spiders, small lizards and birds
animal.habitat: Dense lowland forest and scrub, clinging to vertical trunks
animal.lifespan: ~12 years in the wild; up to ~20 in captivity
animal.size: Body 8.5–16 cm, tail 20–25 cm; 80–160 g
animal.behaviour: By day it sleeps clinging upright to a stem in dense cover. It stresses easily, which is why it does poorly in captivity and under heavy tourism.
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine Tarsier Sanctuary, Corella (Bohol)

lore: The Jesuit naturalist Georg Joseph Kamel described it from the Philippines around 1700, and Linnaeus named it Simia syrichta in 1758 from that account. It is now a symbol of Bohol and its tourism.
funFact: Relative to body size, tarsiers have the largest eyes of any mammal.

summary: The largest toothed predator and owner of the largest brain of any animal, which dives into the deep ocean to hunt squid. Its huge, square head holds the spermaceti organ, which focuses the loudest sounds made by any animal.
nativeRange: Deep waters of all oceans; females and young in tropical and subtropical seas, adult males ranging to polar waters
abilities: Makes echolocation clicks of up to ~230 dB, the loudest sounds known from any animal
Dives to over 2,000 m and stays down for an hour or more
Has a brain of up to ~8–9 kg, the largest known
Families share 'codas', click patterns that identify vocal clans and are now studied for structure
Produces ambergris, a waxy gut secretion formed around indigestible squid beaks

animal.diet: Carnivore: mainly deep-sea squid, including giant squid; also fish
animal.habitat: Deep open ocean, especially over canyons and slopes
animal.size: Males 16–20 m and up to ~45–57 t; females ~11 m and ~15 t
animal.behaviour: Groups sleep for short periods hanging vertically just below the surface. Females form lifelong family units that babysit each other's calves while mothers dive.
fieldMarks: Angled, bushy blow to the left
Low hump instead of a dorsal fin
animal.voice: Loud clicks
animal.lookalikes: Humpback whales have long flippers and a different blow.
animal.whereToSee: Kaikōura (New Zealand), Andenes (Norway) and Dominica

lore: In 1820 a sperm whale rammed and sank the Nantucket whaleship Essex, the event that inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851). Ambergris, called ʿanbar in Arabic, was prized in medieval Islamic and European perfumery and medicine.
funFact: Whalers named it after the waxy spermaceti in its head, which they mistook for sperm.
